sentences.text: Xenovenator is known for its thickened, domed skull roof found in the Campanian Cerro del Pueblo Formation of Coahuila, Mexico.
This structure, formed by the frontal bones, represents a morphology convergent with Pachycephalosauridae, a group of thick-headed dinosaurs.
Martha C. Aguillón-Martínez collected a partial theropod skull during fieldwork in the Cerro del Pueblo Formation at La Parrita, Coahuila, Mexico, in the summer of 2000.
Initially, the partial skull was considered an indeterminate member of the troodontid family and was not named until later.
Martha C. Aguillón-Martínez and Héctor E. Rivera-Sylva formally described specimen CPC 2973 in 2023.
The specific name espinosai honors the Mexican paleontologist and researcher Luis Espinosa.
Xenovenator lived during the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) age, specifically between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
Rivera-Sylva et al. interpreted the dome expansion and fusion as possible evidence of ontogenetic variation, occurring as the animal matured.
An alternative explanation for the dome is sexual dimorphism, an occurrence common in extant mammals and birds but not well-documented in non-avian dinosaurs.

Variation in skull thickening and doming among referred specimens suggests either ontogenetic changes or sexual dimorphism, leading researchers to hypothesize that the skull specializations indicate adaptation for intraspecific combat, specifically head-butting.
Xenovenator is classified in the class Reptilia, the family Troodontidae, and the parent group Troodontini.
Phylogenetic analysis recovered Xenovenator in a late-diverging position within the clade Troodontinae.
This animal inhabited the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
